lead: A single-phase induction motor has one stator winding on the supply. Its field pulses along one axis, not a smooth rotating field. The motor therefore has zero starting torque and needs an auxiliary winding or a shaded pole to begin turning. After it starts, the same winding keeps it running. The universal motor is a series DC motor rebuilt with laminated iron and a compensating winding, so it runs from AC or DC at high speed in small appliances. These are the fractional-kilowatt motors inside fans, refrigerators, mixers and drills.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.5 for the rotating field and slip, and Unit 2 for phase difference and impedance angle.

sections.h3: A pulsating field is two opposite fields

blocks.text: A three-phase winding has three coils spaced 120° apart. Their currents rise and fall in sequence, so the combined field rotates at synchronous speed N<sub>s</sub> = 120f / P, where f is supply frequency in hertz and P is the number of poles. A single-phase motor has only one winding. Its current alternates, so its flux grows, falls and reverses along the same axis. The field pulsates; it does not rotate.
Φ(θ, t) = Φ<sub>m</sub> cos(ωt) cos θ = (Φ<sub>m</sub>/2) cos(θ − ωt) + (Φ<sub>m</sub>/2) cos(θ + ωt)
blocks.where: Φ<sub>m</sub> is peak pulsating flux in weber; θ is space angle around the air gap; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; t is time in second. The first term is the forward field, the second is the backward field.

blocks.text: At standstill the rotor has slip 1 with respect to both fields. The two torques are equal and opposite, so the net starting torque is zero. The motor cannot start alone. If the shaft is pushed, the rotor speed n makes the forward slip s = (N<sub>s</sub> − n)/N<sub>s</sub> and the backward slip s<sub>b</sub> = (N<sub>s</sub> + n)/N<sub>s</sub> = 2 − s. The forward torque then exceeds the backward torque, and the motor accelerates in the direction of the push.

A second winding, called the auxiliary or starting winding, is placed 90 electrical degrees from the main winding in space. If its current is also near 90° away from the main current in time, the two pulsating fields add to a rotating field. The phase split is made by giving the auxiliary winding a different resistance-to-reactance ratio, or by adding a capacitor. A centrifugal switch cuts the auxiliary winding out at about 75% of full speed in most designs.

head: Method
How the phase split is made
Typical use
rows: Auxiliary has high resistance and low reactance; split about 30° to 40°; switch cuts it out.
Series capacitor makes auxiliary current lead; split near 90°; switch cuts auxiliary and capacitor.
Large start capacitor is switched out; small run capacitor stays in circuit for better running power factor.
Copper shading ring delays flux in part of each pole; field sweeps across the pole face.

blocks.text: Resistance split-phase is cheap and gives low starting torque. Capacitor-start gives high starting torque for compressors. Capacitor-start capacitor-run keeps a small capacitor in circuit to improve running power factor and reduce noise. Shaded-pole motors are the simplest and weakest. These motors are small, often below 1 kW, so some syllabi call them fractional-kilowatt or domestic motors.

sections.h3: Universal motor: one series motor for AC and DC

blocks.text: A DC series motor has its field winding in series with the armature, so the same current flows through both. Torque is proportional to Φ Ia, where Φ is the field flux in weber and Ia is the armature current in ampere. On AC, the field current and armature current reverse together. Flux and armature current both change sign, so the torque keeps the same direction. The machine therefore runs on AC as well as DC.

AC operation needs changes. The field magnetic circuit is laminated to reduce eddy currents, because the flux alternates. A compensating winding is placed in the stator to cancel armature magnetomotive force and improve commutation. The motor has brushes and a commutator, so it is not an induction motor. It gives high speed, high starting torque and high power for its size. It is used in mixers, drills, vacuum cleaners and sewing machines. On no load, a series motor can overspeed, so the load should not be removed.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz capacitor-start motor has a main winding whose current lags the supply by 70°. The auxiliary winding alone would lag by 20°. With a 40 μF capacitor in series, its current leads by 15°. Find the phase difference between the two winding currents. State whether the motor will start. Also find the phase split without the capacitor.
steps: Take the supply voltage as the 0° reference. Main winding current angle = −70° (lag).
Auxiliary current angle with the capacitor = +15° (lead).
A rotating field needs a time split close to 90°. 85° is close, so a strong forward field appears; the motor starts.
Without the capacitor, auxiliary current angle = −20°. Phase split = −20° − (−70°) = 50°.
A 50° split gives weak starting torque and unreliable starting for most loads.
examples.answer: The phase difference is 85°, close to the 90° target, so the motor starts; without the capacitor the split is only 50°, too small for reliable starting.
examples.check:
main_lag = 70.0
aux_lead = 15.0
aux_lag_no_cap = 20.0
target = 90.0
phase_split = main_lag + aux_lead
split_no_cap = main_lag - aux_lag_no_cap
print(phase_split)
print(target)
print(split_no_cap)

traps: Calling a single-phase induction motor self-starting: with only the main winding its net starting torque is zero.
Assuming the auxiliary winding always stays in circuit: in resistance split-phase and capacitor-start designs a centrifugal switch cuts it out.
Confusing capacitor-start with capacitor-run: the start capacitor is large and short-time, the run capacitor is small and continuous.
Checking only the 90° space angle: the winding currents must also be near 90° apart in time to make a rotating field.
Treating the universal motor as an induction motor: it has brushes and a commutator, and needs laminated iron and a compensating winding for AC.

quiz.q: What is the net starting torque of a single-phase induction motor with only its main winding connected?
quiz.a: Zero. The forward and backward fields produce equal and opposite torques at standstill.

quiz.q: Why does a single-phase winding produce a pulsating field, not a rotating field?
quiz.a: One winding lies on one axis. Alternating current makes flux rise, fall and reverse along that same axis, with no space displacement between phases.

quiz.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz capacitor-start motor has main current lag 65° and auxiliary current lead 20°. Find the phase split and state whether it is good for starting.
quiz.a: Split = 65° + 20° = 85°. It is close to 90°, so it gives a rotating field and is good for starting.

quiz.q: After the rotor spins, why is backward-field torque smaller than forward-field torque?
quiz.a: Forward slip s is small, backward slip 2 − s is near 2. The backward field has a much larger relative speed and produces much less torque, so the net torque is forward.

quiz.q: Name two starting methods for a single-phase induction motor and one application of each.
quiz.a: Capacitor-start for refrigerator compressors; shaded pole for small fans.

quiz.q: Why does a universal motor run on AC?
quiz.a: Its field and armature are in series. On AC both currents reverse together, so flux and armature current change sign together and torque keeps the same direction.

quiz.q: Why can a universal motor overspeed when the load is removed?
quiz.a: It is a series motor. Low load means low current and weak flux, so speed rises until back EMF balances the supply; the speed can become dangerously high.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern appliances increasingly use brushless DC motors because they are more efficient and last longer. The single-phase induction motor remains cheap and robust for fixed-speed domestic loads. Search next for double-revolving-field theory, split-phase motor starting, and universal-motor compensating windings. Motor efficiency classes for small motors are also worth reading.
